title: Young Colum and Starkey. George Roberts is doing the commercial part. Longworth will give it a good puff in the Express. O, will he? I liked Colum’s Drover. Yes, I think he has that queer thing genius. Do you think he has genius really? Yeats admired his line: As in wild earth a Grecian vase. Did he? I hope you’ll be able to come tonight. Malachi Mulligan is coming too. Moore asked him to bring Haines. Did you hear Miss Mitchell’s joke about Moore and Martyn? That Moore is Martyn’s wild oats? Awfully clever, isn’t it? They remind one of Don Quixote and Sancho Panza. Our national epic has yet to be written, Dr Sigerson says. Moore is the man for it. A knight of the rueful countenance here in Dublin. With a saffron kilt? O’Neill Russell? O, yes, he must speak the grand old tongue. And his Dulcinea? James Stephens is doing some clever sketches. We are becoming important, it seems.
html_source:
Termed telegraphic external narrative
ie the conversations in the room.
Gifford p212-213:
Young Colum – Padraic Colum, irish poet.
Starkey – Irish poet.
George Roberts – poet & publisher.
Longworth – editor of the Daily Express

(Gabriel in The Dead writes for the Express).
Sigerson – scientist and man of letters had stated that Ireland had contributed to other epics rather than having its own.

Susan Mitchell- wit and associate editor of Irish Homesteads.

The joke and Don Quixote and Sancho Panza refer to the relationship between George Moore and Edward Martyn. They were cousins and Martyn , a wealthy landlord supported the author Moore and the Irish revival. They didn’t always get on !

This is the second allusion to Cervantes in this national library episode – the other being La Gitanilla.
A knight if the rueful countenance – Cervantes epithet for Don Quixote
Saffron kilt – thought by some to be worn in ancient Ireland
Thomas O'Neil Russell – a figure in the Celtic /language revival
The he is the hero of our national epic.
Dulcinea – a girl, Aldonzo Lorenzo, for whom Don Q had the hots.
James Stephens – Irish poet.
